title: AutoVLA-D: Learning a Trajectory-Geometric Condition from Reasoning for VLA Planning
claim: A two-stage pipeline first learns a discrete geometric condition from reasoning inputs, then conditions final continuous prediction on it.
layout: 4 columns, left-to-right; stage panels share a VLA backbone with fire icons
description: A wide four-column pipeline diagram with a legend strip at the bottom. The left column shows inputs: a front-view driving photo labeled 'Observed image o' and a text box with the driving instruction. The second, purple-bordered column, 'Discrete TrajCond GT', stacks boxes top to bottom, linked by arrows. It runs from an explicit continuous trajectory, to dynamic reference local motion with Δx, Δy and Δθ, to 1D-Brohan discretization with x, y and θ codebooks, and ends in TrajCond action tokens. The two gold-bordered panels, Stage-1 and Stage-2, each show image, instruction and token embeddings feeding a 'Multimodal VLA Model' with a flame icon. Stage-1 outputs predicted TrajCond action tokens under SFT supervision. Stage-2 adds teacher-forced TrajCond tokens and outputs the continuous trajectory. Purple, green and pink tokens mark the modalities. The legend explains flame, supervision arrow, token colors, inputs and teacher forcing.
caption: Pipeline of AutoVLA-D.
abstract: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with \textit{TrajCond}, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method \textbf{AutoVLA-D} (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/AutoVLA-D.
